rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Korah attributes his blessings to knowledge he possesses, rather than acknowledging them as divine gifts.
rows.anchor: it is clear that Korah attributes the blessings he possesses to knowledge he has

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators explain Korah’s wealth through particular skills; accounts call him a goldsmith or alchemist, though commentators mention and dismiss both accounts.
rows.anchor: Some say he was a goldsmith; others transmit a tradition that he was an alchemist, which are both mentioned and dismissed by commentators

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere ʿalā ʿilm can mean that God acts on the basis of His Knowledge; its sense in other cases remains open to interpretation.
rows.anchor: in other instances this phrase can also be used to mean that God acts based upon His Knowledge

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some commentators take ʿindī to mean “in my opinion,” yielding “given on account of knowledge, in my opinion.”
rows.anchor: the word and which would make the translation, “I have only been given it on account of knowledge, in my opinion”(R, Ṭ)

words: أَوَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ قَدْ أَهْلَكَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning about earlier peoples as strong or wealthy as Korah who were destroyed recurs in several verses.
rows.anchor: Other verses in which disbelievers are reminded of those generations or peoples who came before them

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One reading is that the guilty of one generation are not questioned about or held responsible for another generation’s sins.
rows.anchor: the guilty of one generation will not be questioned about or held responsible for the sins of another generation (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The statement can mean that the guilty cannot make amends or obtain favor, paralleling 30:57 and 41:24.
rows.anchor: Nor can they make amends (Q); and 41:24: And if they seek favor, they will not be granted favor

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God has no need to question the guilty about their deeds because He already knows them completely.
rows.anchor: God has no need to question them about their deeds, because He already knows these deeds completely (R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: To reconcile this with 15:92, some distinguish questions seeking information, calling to account, or rebuking; God questions people in one respect, not another.
rows.anchor: different kinds of questions to be asked—those that seek information, those that call one to account, and those that are meant as rebuke (R)

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Sufis counsel against exulting in one’s attainments or taking pride in one’s states, words, or deeds; such self-glorification marks a wretched person.
rows.anchor: According to the Sufis, one should not exult in one’s own attainments or be pleased with one’s own state

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Commentators relate that Korah’s enmity, rebellion, and slander against Moses led God to grant Moses power to call for the earth to swallow Korah.
rows.anchor: God granted the latter the power to call upon the earth to swallow him (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fiʾah, rendered “party,” can denote a group one can call upon for support in battle.
rows.anchor: refers to a group upon whom one can call for support in a battle (see 8:15–16c)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some take kaʾanna in the repeated phrase as emphatic, or supply an implicit verb such as “Know” or “Do you not know.”
rows.anchor: that] God outspreads” or “Alas! [Do you not know that] God outspreads?” (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Another vocalization permits the sense “Alas for you! Truly God outspreads.”
rows.anchor: Others read this phrase as meaning, “Alas for you! Truly God outspreads,” which is possible depending on how the letters are voweled (Q, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s expanding and constricting provision is also mentioned in several other verses.
rows.anchor: The idea that God outspreads and straitens also appears in 13:26; 17:30; 29:62; 30:37; 34:36, 39; 39:52

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “And morning found those” can simply mean “and it came to be that those.”
rows.anchor: And morning found those could also mean simply “and it came to be that those.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeats Abraham’s story in over two hundred verses and presents Islam as a renewal of his creed, which Muslims are instructed to follow and invoke when defining their faith.
rows.anchor: Various aspects of Abraham’s story are repeated in over two hundred verses of the Quran. Islam presents itself as the renewal of his creed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s command to worship and reverence God summarizes his longer appeals in several other passages.
rows.anchor: The injunction to worship God and reverence Him is a summation of Abraham’s more extensive entreaties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham criticizes his father’s idol worship elsewhere, while his father and people justify it by saying they follow their ancestors.
rows.anchor: His criticism of their idol worship is found in several accounts, as when he chastises his father, saying, Do you take idols for gods?

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: “Creating perversion” means lying by claiming that the idols are gods.
rows.anchor: That they only create perversion refers to their lie in claiming that their idols are gods (IJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols cannot provide sustenance, exposing their worship as futile; they are not even lesser intermediaries bringing worshippers near to God, as idolaters claim, and Jesus makes a similar argument.
rows.anchor: That the idols they worship have no power over what provision may come (cf. 16:73) indicates the utter futility of their worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return to God refers to the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: speaks to the promise of the Resurrection; see 2:28c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot is considered either Abraham’s nephew or cousin; the Quranic narrative has parallels in several passages and in Genesis 19.
rows.anchor: For other narrative accounts of Lot (who is considered to be either Abraham’s nephew or cousin)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s flight from Sodom means emigrating wherever God provides refuge, paralleling the first Muslims’ emigration for God’s sake and the greater reward promised for it.
rows.anchor: Lot’s declaration I am fleeing unto my Lord indicates that he is emigrating from Sodom to wherever God will provide him refuge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse can extend the theme of 29:10, read as addressing Muslims who failed to emigrate, suffered affliction, and nearly apostatized.
rows.anchor: The present verse can thus be read as an extension of the theme in v. 10

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun “him” in the verse refers to Abraham.
rows.anchor: Here him refers to Abraham.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isaac and Jacob are described as divine gifts elsewhere; Jacob is an additional gift because Ishmael was born before Isaac.
rows.anchor: Isaac and Jacob are also identified as Divine gifts in 6:84 and 19:49 and referred to as an added gift in 21:72

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The news that Abraham and Sarah would have Isaac is recounted in other passages.
rows.anchor: For the account of Abraham and his wife, Sarah, receiving the news of Isaac’s impending birth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Lot narrative is also related in other Quranic accounts and Genesis 19.
rows.anchor: For the story of Lot, who was sent to the people of Sodom, see 7:80–84; 11:77–83; 15:57–77

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fāḥishah, rendered “indecency,” denotes an abominable sin and most often refers to sexual transgression.
rows.anchor: which denotes an abominable sin and is most often used with reference to sexual transgression

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Here the indecency specifically means sex between men; commentators say no people before Lot’s people committed it so widely.
rows.anchor: a transgression that, based upon this verse, commentators say no people had committed on such a wide scale before Lot’s people (IK; cf. 7:81)

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Given the aggressive approaches described in other accounts, some maintain that Lot reproaches the men for forcible rather than consensual sex.
rows.anchor: some maintain that Lot reproaches them for forcible rather than consensual sexual relations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphasis in this verse and parallels is on approaching men with desire and lust, whether the relations are consensual or not.
rows.anchor: However, the emphasis here and in 7:81; 26:165–66, and 27:54 is upon approaching men with desire and lust, whether consensual or not

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: “Cutting off the way” can mean that preferring men over women blocks the way to having children.
rows.anchor: preferring men over women means they cut off the way to having children (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, they cut off travelers’ way; some accounts say they specifically targeted travelers for rape.
rows.anchor: or they cut off the way of travelers, as, according to some accounts, they specifically targeted travelers to rape them(Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people’s challenge to Lot resembles challenges made by the ʿĀd to Hūd and the Thamūd to Ṣāliḥ.
rows.anchor: Their challenge to Lot is similar to the one the ʿĀd pose to the prophet Hūd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Working corruption” is elsewhere associated more generally with physical violence.
rows.anchor: “working corruption” is connected in a more general manner to committing physical violence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In other verses, corruption often combines spiritual and worldly corruption; the Quran’s conception of corruption is discussed at 30:41.
rows.anchor: In other verses, it often implies a combination of spiritual and worldly corruption

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This town” refers to Sodom and Gomorrah; the angels’ visit to Abraham is also mentioned in several passages.
rows.anchor: This town refers to the towns of Sodom and Gomorrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham pleads about Lot’s people elsewhere; the angels say they will destroy the town but save Lot and his family, except his wife.
rows.anchor: the angels explain that they will destroy everyone in it, save for the family of Lot . . . except for his wife

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “We know better who is in it” means the angels know better than Abraham which inhabitants are wrongdoers or believers; Lot is not among the wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: they know better than Abraham who the wrongdoers and believers are, and that Lot is not among the wrongdoers (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghābirīn means those left behind, destroyed in this life and covered with dust, then disgraced with dust-covered faces and darkness in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Those who lagged behind renders ghābirīn and indicates that they are destroyed in this life, completely covered over by dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rijz can mean defilement or plague, but most likely refers to the baked-clay or torrent of stones said to have rained upon Lot’s people.
rows.anchor: Torment, which also appears in 2:59 and 7:134, renders rijz, a word that can also be understood to mean “defilement,”

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The punishment left by God is a sign, proof, and warning for people who understand.
rows.anchor: God has left the punishment that He inflicted upon the people of Lot as a sign, a proof and a warning, for those who understand (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The sign may be the town’s ruins, the stones or rain that fell upon it, or the account of Lot’s people.
rows.anchor: It could refer to the ruins of their town, the stones or rain that came down upon them, or the account of their story (Z)

rows.speaker: IJ, Q, R
rows.claim: “Prayer” here refers to the obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: Here prayer refers to the obligatory prayers (IJ, Q, R)

words: ٱتْلُ مَآ أُوحِىَ إِلَيْكَ مِنَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ
rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some interpret “prayer” as Quran recitation, a form of supererogatory worship; al-Rāzī rejects this because the verse already commands Quran recitation.
rows.anchor: Some say it means the act of reciting the Quran (IJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues against interpreting prayer as recitation because the verse has already mentioned reciting the Quran.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī argues against such an interpretation, given that the verse already begins with the mention of reciting the Quran

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: The paired commands may mean that prayer prevents sin when one reflects on the Quran recited during it.
rows.anchor: The combined command to recite the Quran and perform the prayer can be understood to mean that if one performs the prayers and then reflects upon the words of the Quran recited in them

words: إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: Others understand prayer in and of itself to prevent indecency and abomination.
rows.anchor: though others understand this verse to mean that prayer in and of itself fulfills this function (IJ)

words: إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: Prophet / Ibn Masʿūd
rows.claim: A saying, variously attributed to the Prophet or his Companion Ibn Masʿūd, says prayer that fails to prevent indecency and abomination only increases distance from God.
rows.anchor: According to a saying sometimes attributed to the Prophet and sometimes to his Companion Ibn Masʿūd

words: إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Prayer may not prevent sin without sincerity and repentance; God accepts only from the reverent, as 5:27 says.
rows.anchor: prayer in and of itself may not prevent indecency and abomination unless it is combined with sincerity and repentance, as in 5:27

words: إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet says a young man who prayed with him but inclined toward indecency would soon be restrained by his prayer.
rows.anchor: Surely his prayer will soon prevent him [from doing that]” (Bḍ, Q, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Indecency may mean fornication, while abomination may mean disobedience.
rows.anchor: Here indecency may refer to fornication and abomination to disobedience (Ṭ)

words: إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet compares the five daily prayers to washing in a river five times daily: prayer removes one’s sins just as washing removes filth.
rows.anchor: the Prophet asked his Companions, “Tell me, if one of you had a river at his door in which he washed five times a day

rows.speaker: al-Ghazzālī
rows.claim: Al-Ghazzālī says prayer was prescribed to polish the heart and renew remembrance of God, not merely to perform its words and motions.
rows.anchor: al-Ghazzālī advises penetrating deeper into prayer, since it was not prescribed merely for the words and motions it entails

words: إِنَّ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ تَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ
rows.speaker: al-Tustarī
rows.claim: Al-Tustarī says prayer that does not restrain shameful and unjust acts, and lacks the adornment of shunning them, is tainted and must be purified.
rows.anchor: al-Tustarī is reported to have said, “Every prayer that does not restrain shameful and unjust deeds

rows.speaker: IJ, Sh, Ṭ
rows.claim: One meaning is that remembering God is greater than everything else, including other acts of worship.
rows.anchor: The remembrance of God is surely greater (or “greatest”) means that to remember God is greater than all else (IJ, Sh, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IJ, Sh, Su, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: Another meaning is that God’s remembrance of human beings exceeds their remembrance of Him.
rows.anchor: From another perspective, it means that God’s remembrance of human beings is greater than their remembrance of God (Bḍ, IJ, Sh, Su, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: This reading is explained by God’s remembrance being eternal while human remembrance is temporal.
rows.anchor: since His remembrance is eternal and theirs is temporal (Su)

rows.speaker: Sh, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some hold that both the believer’s remembrance of God and God’s remembrance of believers are meant at once.
rows.anchor: or both meanings can obtain at the same time (Sh, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufi interpretation joins both senses: full remembrance requires annihilation of selfhood, so God remembers Himself through people beyond time and place.
rows.anchor: From a Sufi perspective, the two meanings together indicate that the fullness of remembrance comes only when individuals have been annihilated before God

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some read the phrase to mean that remembering God during prayer is greater than the indecency and abomination prayer prevents.
rows.anchor: Some also understand this verse to mean that remembering God in prayer is better than the indecency and abomination that it prevents (IJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another reading is that believers’ remembrance of God is greater than idolaters’ remembrance of their gods.
rows.anchor: that believers’remembrance of God is better than idolaters’ remembrance of their gods (R)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Z
rows.claim: A further reading takes “remembrance of God” as prayer, which is greater than every other act of obedience.
rows.anchor: what is meant by the remembrance of God in this verse, is better than all other acts of obedience (Bḍ, Z)

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that the world and everything in it are accursed except remembrance of God and what supports it.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said, “The world is accursed, accursed is all that is in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that God first composes human beings from dust and then resurrects them.
rows.anchor: the composition of human beings from dust and their resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase concerns the beginning of all creation and the eventual return of all things to God.
rows.anchor: the beginning of all creation and the eventual return of all things to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return to God refers to the Resurrection and the return of all things to Him.
rows.anchor: Then unto Him shall you be returned (cf. 2:28, 245; 10:56; 11:34; 21:35

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: “That you see” may refer to the pillars, as translated, or to the heavens: “you see them without pillars.”
rows.anchor: As translated, that you see refers to pillars. But it could also be understood as a reference to the heavens

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about God placing firm mountains in the earth is discussed further at 16:15.
rows.anchor: Regarding cast into the earth firm mountains, see 16:15c.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Spreading beasts across the earth shows God’s Mercy in providing nourishment.
rows.anchor: That God has spread about all manner of beast (cf. 2:164) upon the earth indicates God’s Mercy in providing nourishment (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The spread of animals across the earth also demonstrates the extent of God’s Knowledge and Power.
rows.anchor: and the extent of His Knowledge and Power (IK)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “Beast” can mean all animals, while “every noble kind” can mean every kind of vegetation.
rows.anchor: Beast can be understood as a reference to all animals, and every noble kind (cf. 26:7) can be understood as a reference to every form of vegetation (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Karīm also means “generous”; some take it to describe vegetation that gives abundantly without asking anything in return.
rows.anchor: Noble translates karīm, which also means “generous” and is thus understood by some as a reference to the manner in which vegetation gives abundantly without asking anything in return (R)
